name: Image I/O (CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex)
baseline: UIGraphicsImageRenderer drawing a full UIImage(contentsOfFile:) into a smaller context
verdict_reason: The common advice to resize with ImageIO thumbnails is about memory, not time: NSHipster's iPhone 7 test timed ImageIO at 0.1616 s against 0.1420 s for UIGraphicsImageRenderer. Nuke's docs report thumbnails up to 4x faster than its own resize processor, but only for high-resolution images and without published data.
tier_reason: Independent measurement (NSHipster) with public code and the device and OS stated, run in the Debug test configuration.
claimed_speedup: NSHipster (iPhone 7, iOS 12.2): Image I/O 0.1616 s vs UIKit 0.1420 s (UIKit about 12% faster, derived from page data). Nuke: thumbnail decoding 'up to 4x faster' than its Resize processor for high-resolution images. Downsampling in general: 23.7 MB vs 220.2 MB memory.
workload: Load a 12,000 px square, 20 MB JPEG from disk, scale it to 100 x 100 and return a UIImage; average of XCTest measure() iterations.
toolchain: Swift 5.0; Debug test configuration in the example project's scheme
one_liner: ImageIO's thumbnail call cuts decode memory by about 10x, but timed no faster than UIGraphicsImageRenderer in an iPhone 7 test.
how_it_is_fast: CGImageSourceCreateThumbnailAtIndex decodes to a requested maximum pixel size, using an embedded thumbnail when the file has one, so a full-size bitmap need not be kept. Drawing with UIGraphicsImageRenderer creates an image from the full file and rasterizes it into the small context; in NSHipster's test that was not slower, and the article does not say why.
use_it_when: Memory matters: downsampling a 12,000 px image cut memory from 220.2 MB to 23.7 MB in NSHipster's test
Making thumbnails off the main thread straight from a file URL or Data without creating a UIImage first
Camera JPEGs with embedded thumbnails, where Nuke reports its largest gains
skip_it_when: Expecting a speed win over UIGraphicsImageRenderer for ordinary resizing: the independent test showed none
You need an exact output size or crop; the API fits the image within a maximum pixel size
caveats: NSHipster ran its XCTest benchmarks in the Debug configuration; the timed work is almost all inside Apple's compiled frameworks, so the effect is likely small, but it is still a debug build
iPhone 7 with iOS 12.2 (2019); no newer device measurement found
Nuke's 'up to 4x' comes with no data, device or image set
The memory table is for downsampling in general, not for the ImageIO technique alone
Apple's WWDC 2018 session 219 on downsampling, cited by NSHipster, now redirects to the WWDC18 index
tradeoffs: CoreFoundation-style API configured through option dictionaries
Output is bounded by a maximum pixel size rather than an exact target size

evidence.quote: performed on an iPhone 7 running iOS 12.2,
this image measures 12,000 px square and weighs in at a whopping 20 MB.
It can be up to 4x faster than using ``ImageProcessors/Resize`` for high-resolution images.
